name: OfficialEntry
idea: A hand-verified directory of the one official website for every ETA, e-visa and arrival card, with scam-lookalike warnings.
description: Travellers pick a destination and get the official government URL for its ETA, e-visa, digital arrival card or e-declaration, whether it is free or paid, who needs it, how early to file, and a last-verified date. A 'Is this site official?' check compares a pasted URL with the curated allowlist. The moat is the verified, dated dataset: several governments do not index their own portals, so scam resellers outrank them and nobody has a clean source of truth.
web_delivery: Static-first Next.js pages on Vercel Hobby (one SEO page per country and document) reading a Supabase table with source_url, official_domain, fee, verified_at; a 'report a change' form writes to Supabase.
why_hard_to_copy: Hand-curated and dated registry of official portals (checked against embassy and ministry pages), plus a change log; scrapers cannot do it because many official portals are unindexed and the lookalike scam sites rank above them.

name: TransitCheck
idea: Tell a traveller whether a given passport needs a visa to transit a specific airport, airside or landside, single ticket or separate.
description: User enters passport nationality, any valid visas or residence permits, transit airport, and whether the legs are one ticket or self-transfer; the tool returns a verdict with the cited rule (Schengen airport transit visa lists, UK DATV, Canada transit, ETIAS airside exemption) and caveats. The moat is a sourced per-country rules table with last-verified dates, because the answer changes by nationality, visa held, ticket type and airport zone.
web_delivery: Next.js on Vercel with a Supabase rules table (country, nationality group, exemption conditions, source URL, verified_at); evaluation runs in the browser.
why_hard_to_copy: Correctness-critical rules engine over a hand-curated, cited dataset that changes often (nationality lists, exemptions for US/Schengen/UK visa holders); asking in forums is the current workaround because Timatic is paid.

web_delivery: Next.js on Vercel; per-airport step times and terminal-transfer notes in Supabase; calculation client-side.
why_hard_to_copy: Curated per-airport procedure data (terminal transfer routes, recheck and immigration rules, bag-drop closing times) that airlines do not publish for self-transfers.

name: AirportRules
idea: Per-airport quick facts that general travel sites do not track: liquids limit status, exit-from-transit feasibility, left-luggage and bag-drop hours.
description: Each airport page shows whether the 100 ml liquids rule is still enforced (and which lanes use CT scanners), whether passengers can leave the departures or transit area, left-luggage and large-item storage options with hours, and earliest bag-drop time, each with a source link and verified date. Users can submit corrections. The moat is a hand-curated, dated, community-corrected dataset; the facts live on scattered airport pages and are only partly covered by news roundups.
web_delivery: Next.js on Vercel reading Supabase tables (airport, rule, source_url, verified_at); logged-in-free correction form with moderation queue.
why_hard_to_copy: Dated, sourced per-airport facts maintained by curation and user corrections; each fact must be verified at the airport's own page so it cannot be generated from a template.

name: TicketName
idea: Show exactly how to type a long, multi-part or single name on an airline booking so it matches the passport.
description: User enters passport name parts and the airline; the tool outputs the first-name and last-name fields to use, handles field-length limits, single names (FNU/LNU conventions), suffixes, hyphens and missing middle names, and tells how risky the mismatch is. Includes a similar helper for two-field visa forms with Arabic and other multi-part names. The moat is a curated, airline-by-airline rules table; the logic has many edge cases that general advice pages skip.
web_delivery: Next.js on Vercel; rules in Supabase (airline, max_chars, single_name_format, suffix_rule, source_url); pure client-side formatter.
why_hard_to_copy: Correctness-critical, hand-sourced airline and GDS name-field rules and edge-case logic (mononyms, double surnames, diacritics, length truncation) with citations to each carrier's own guidance.

name: BackupPowerPlanner

why_hard_to_copy: Curated appliance start-up and duty-cycle dataset, inverter and cord derating, plus NEC-style wire, breaker and interlock logic; error-prone for hobbyists to rebuild correctly.

name: MiterReach
idea: Check whether a given mitre saw can make a specific cut, including angled cuts and flip cuts.
description: User enters the saw model (or blade size and slide travel) and the board profile and angles; the tool shows the maximum crosscut and height at that miter and bevel, whether a flip cut works, and the clearance needed. The moat is a hand-collected saw-capacity table from manuals plus geometry, which published 'max cut' specs hide.
web_delivery: Next.js on Vercel; saw specs in Supabase; geometry rendered client-side as a 2D diagram.
why_hard_to_copy: Per-model capacity data at angles (mostly in PDF manuals) combined with cut geometry; buyers cannot get this from spec sheets that quote only 0-degree capacity.

signals.summary: Asker needs to cut 220 mm x 90 mm PVC ducting and cannot tell whether a mitre saw with a smaller listed crosscut can do it, including with a flip cut.
DIYer asks whether a 10-inch mitre saw can cut a 56-degree bevel in a 2x6.

competitors_seen.name: Omni Calculator miter angle
competitors_seen.note: Calculates angles to set, not saw cut capacity.

marketing.target: Buyers choosing a mitre saw; DIY carpenters
marketing.funnel: Search 'can my miter saw cut a 2x12' -> tool.
marketing.cold_outreach: Offer tool-review blogs a capacity widget per model.
post_ideas: Can a 10-inch mitre saw cut a 2x6 at 56 degrees?
Flip cuts: how wide a board you can really cut
Saw capacity cheat sheet by model

notes: Two signals, low-moderate views (744 and 1,109) and a niche audience. Included because the moat (curated per-model data) is real but demand is thin; likely better as a feature of a larger tool-buying site.

name: SafeCanning
idea: A canning planner that applies altitude, jar size and acidity rules to tested recipes and warns when a change makes it unsafe.
description: User picks a tested recipe family and altitude; the tool gives adjusted water-bath times or canner pressures, headspace and jar-size notes, and flags changes such as reduced sugar, added low-acid ingredients or process interruptions. It reproduces published USDA and extension tables and refuses to guess for untested changes. The moat is the careful, cited rules table and decision logic.
web_delivery: Next.js PWA on Vercel; tables from public tested-recipe sources in Supabase; works offline in kitchens.
why_hard_to_copy: Correctness-critical, cited processing tables and 'is this change safe?' decision logic; hard to get right and not a weekend CRUD build.

signals.summary: Asker is unsure what 'low-acid food' means for water-bath versus pressure canning and wants authority citations.
Home canner forgot to cook salsa before steam canning and asks whether to discard it.
Home cook reduced sugar in strawberry preserves and asks about botulism risk in the refrigerator jam.
Canner ran out of propane 10 minutes before the end of a 75-minute pressure process on beef stew and asks if it must be reprocessed.
Jelly maker gets about half the stated yield from a pectin jelly recipe and asks why.
Candy maker wants the science of adjusting temperatures for high altitude.

competitors_seen.name: UC Master Food Preserver altitude guidance
competitors_seen.note: Extension document with altitude tables; not an interactive tool.

competitors_seen.name: USU Utah altitude adjustments for home canning
competitors_seen.note: Static PDF.

competitors_seen.name: National Center for Home Food Preservation
competitors_seen.note: Authoritative recipes and guides; web search found no altitude/jar calculator from them.

satellite.name: Altitude Time Adder
satellite.what: Simple altitude-to-extra-minutes table for water-bath canning with source links.
satellite.why_shared: Frequently needed and easy to bookmark.
satellite.handoff: Links to the full SafeCanning planner for recipe-specific adjustments.

marketing.target: Home canners, gardeners with seasonal gluts, homesteaders
marketing.funnel: Search 'canning altitude adjustment calculator' -> tool.
marketing.cold_outreach: Offer extension educators a link for handouts.
post_ideas: Altitude adjustment for water-bath canning in one table
Did you change the sugar? Is the jam still safe to can?
What to do when the canner pressure drops mid-process

notes: Six different asks over the window. Strong liability angle: must stick to published tested values, show sources and tell users to discard when unsure. Several questions are 'is this safe?' rather than tool requests, so demand for a tool is inferred.

name: RecipeFixer
idea: Adapt a recipe to what you have: smart scaling, tiny-amount conversions and context-aware substitutions.
description: Paste or enter a recipe and a target (half batch, different pan, missing ingredient); the tool scales eggs by weight, adjusts leavening and spice non-linearly, rounds tiny amounts to real packet or spoon sizes, flags prep ambiguity such as measure-before-grinding, and suggests substitutions that depend on the dish type. The moat is the baking-science rules and substitution matrix, not a linear multiplier.
web_delivery: Next.js PWA on Vercel; rules in Supabase; all calculations client-side.
why_hard_to_copy: Curated non-linear scaling rules and a dish-aware substitution matrix; plain multipliers are trivial, this is not.

signals.summary: Baker wants to halve a large cake recipe and asks about layer sizes and baking times.
Pizza recipe calls for 0.09 oz of yeast and the asker does not know how many 0.25 oz packets that is.
Muffin recipe says '1 c. cereal, ground' and the asker does not know whether to measure before or after grinding.
Cook has ground basil instead of the 12 fresh leaves a recipe needs and asks for a conversion.
Asker wants to know whether chickpea flour and besan are interchangeable.
Person with an egg intolerance wants substitutes that work for scrambled eggs and omelets, not just baking.

competitors_seen.name: Instacart recipe converter
competitors_seen.note: Basic scaling by servings.

competitors_seen.name: RecipeSage pan converter
competitors_seen.note: Pan-size multiplier only.

competitors_seen.name: Omni Calculator fresh-to-dry herb conversion
competitors_seen.note: Single conversion table, not dish-aware.

satellite.name: Yeast Packet Converter
satellite.what: Convert ounces or grams of yeast to packets or teaspoons and halve eggs correctly.
satellite.why_shared: One-off questions that spark search traffic.
satellite.handoff: Links to RecipeFixer for full recipes.

marketing.target: Home bakers and cooks adapting recipes
marketing.funnel: Search 'how to halve a cake recipe' -> tool.
marketing.cold_outreach: Offer recipe bloggers a free scaling widget.
post_ideas: How to halve a cake recipe without ruining it
0.09 oz of yeast is how many packets?
Fresh to dried herbs: when the ratio breaks

notes: Many scalers exist; the differentiator is non-linear rules, which a motivated vibe coder could partly copy. Substitution data needs expert curation. Signals are low-engagement (141-2,223 views).

name: GadgetRecipes
idea: Find recipes by the kitchen equipment you own rather than by ingredient.
description: A community-tagged index of recipe links by equipment (meat grinder, ice cream maker, pasta extruder, bread machine), filterable and linked out to the original source so no recipe text is copied. The moat is the community-curated tag set; search engines return product pages and low-quality content for 'recipes using X'.
web_delivery: Next.js on Vercel; Supabase tables for recipe links, equipment tags, votes; no image hosting.
why_hard_to_copy: Community-curated equipment tagging of links (a small-network effect), not machine-generated; but a thin moat until it has contributors.

signals.summary: Asker buys single-purpose gadgets reluctantly and cannot find any site that filters recipes by equipment, while web searches return slop and shopping pages.

competitors_seen.name: Instant Pot Eats air fryer recipes
competitors_seen.note: Single-appliance blog collections; web search found no multi-appliance filter.

marketing.target: Owners of specialty kitchen equipment
marketing.funnel: Search 'recipes for <gadget>' -> equipment page.
marketing.cold_outreach: Invite appliance-owner group moderators to seed tags.
post_ideas: What can you make with a meat grinder besides sausage?
Bread machine: 20 recipes beyond loaves
Share your best recipe for an ice cream maker

notes: Single signal (371 views, 4 score). Included only because the stated gap (no equipment filter) was confirmed by search; a vibe coder could build the shell quickly and the moat is community, so treat as speculative.

name: DateCodeDecoder
idea: Decode lot and date codes printed on food packages by brand.
description: User enters a brand and the stamped code and gets the likely production or expiry date, using a crowd-curated table of per-manufacturer formats (Julian dates, plant codes, month letters) plus links to shelf-life guidance. The moat is the crowd-built format library, which does not exist in one place; manufacturers publish only fragments.
web_delivery: Next.js on Vercel; format rules (pattern, example, source) in Supabase; decoder runs in the browser.
why_hard_to_copy: Community- and expert-curated library of brand-specific code formats; each entry needs real packages as evidence.

signals.summary: Shopper tries to interpret a code like A164 24164/2 Z1 on a box of sesame snaps bought price-reduced in Ontario.

competitors_seen.name: Hormel: code dates decoded
competitors_seen.note: One manufacturer's explanation; web search found no universal decoder.

where: Food safety and grocery-shopping Facebook groups
marketing.target: Shoppers checking reduced items and old pantry goods
marketing.funnel: Search '<brand> date code meaning' -> brand page.
marketing.cold_outreach: Ask consumer-advice writers to contribute formats.
post_ideas: How to read the date code on <brand> products
Julian date codes explained with 10 examples
Reduced-price shelf: is it actually expired?

notes: One signal with little engagement (266 views, 5 score). Dataset-driven moat, but demand evidence is the weakest in my set; included as an honest low-confidence idea.

name: BikeFit
idea: A bike-parts compatibility checker for standards, sizes and capacities.
description: User enters frame and drivetrain details and a target part; the tool checks bottom-bracket shell width and standard, cassette versus rear-derailleur capacity, chain length, tyre and rim width limits, and inch-versus-ETRTO tube sizes, and explains why. The moat is a curated cross-brand standards dataset with correctness-critical rules; manufacturers publish only their own parts.
web_delivery: Next.js on Vercel; component standards and rule tables in Supabase; checks client-side.
why_hard_to_copy: Cross-brand standards dataset (BB shells, freehub splines, RD capacity, ETRTO) plus formula logic for chain length and clearance; needs cycling expertise.

signals.summary: Asker notes a manufacturer ships a bike with tyres wider than the frame's own maximum tyre size.

competitors_seen.note: Brand-only compatibility.

name: OldRecordDecoder
idea: A searchable glossary and symbol guide for decoding old genealogy records: abbreviations, column codes, old scripts and register marks.
description: Users look up a record type and place (for example a UK 1939 Register annotation, a US church record index volume code, a Latin or French parish baptism entry, or Kurrent handwriting) and get a decoder with examples and links to sources. The moat is an expert-curated, cross-referenced glossary tied to record collections, built from genealogists' knowledge rather than generic dictionaries.
web_delivery: Next.js on Vercel; glossary entries, example images (small, linked) and sources in Supabase.
why_hard_to_copy: Expert-curated cross-collection glossary and example library; general OCR or AI transcription is unreliable for these scripts, so a reference people trust is the product.

name: NightTransfer
idea: A guide to getting to and from airports and between airports when trains and buses have stopped.
description: For major airports and city pairs, the page lists last and first services, night buses, taxi or fixed-price options, accessible routes with luggage, and whether you can stay in the airport overnight. The moat is a curated and dated dataset of off-hours alternatives, which general map apps handle poorly and that changes seasonally.
web_delivery: Next.js on Vercel; Supabase tables of airport, mode, last/first service, source URL and verified_at.
why_hard_to_copy: Hand-checked off-hours service data for airports and inter-airport transfers; maps and trip planners return nothing useful after midnight.
